A Tutorial: Clustering Anonymized Mixed Data with MixClustVIjl

A worked example on the UCI Australian Credit Approval dataset — draft companion tutorial, to be published once the manuscript is posted to arXiv

Status note (remove before publishing). This is a draft tutorial, written to accompany the paper Local Feature Relevance and Cluster Order Selection in Model-Based Clustering for Mixed Data via Variational Inference. It is not part of the manuscript itself and is held back from publication until the paper is posted to arXiv.

1 What This Tutorial Covers

The Iris tutorial showed the package on a small, well-understood continuous dataset. This one stress-tests a different axis: how does MixClustVIjl perform when most features are categorical, some with many levels, and none carry any usable semantic meaning? The UCI Statlog Australian Credit Approval dataset is built for exactly this kind of test — and unlike Iris, it comes with a genuine binary outcome label (loan approved/rejected), so we can compute an Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) against external ground truth.

2 The Dataset

This dataset concerns credit card applications. Per the UCI documentation: “All attribute names and values have been changed to meaningless symbols to protect confidentiality of the data.” It has \(n=690\) applications, 6 continuous and 8 categorical attributes (A1–A14), and a binary class label (1 = approved, 0 = rejected; 307 approved, 383 rejected). Missing values (5% of cases) were imputed in the standard release used here (mode for categorical, mean for continuous).

Attribute Type Levels / notes
A1 categorical 2 levels
A2 continuous
A3 continuous
A4 categorical 3 levels
A5 categorical 14 levels
A6 categorical 8 levels
A7 continuous
A8 categorical 2 levels
A9 categorical 2 levels
A10 continuous integer-valued, zero-inflated (median 0, max 67)
A11 categorical 2 levels
A12 categorical 3 levels
A13 continuous
A14 continuous extreme right skew — log1p-transformed before standardization
class label (not a feature) 1 = approved, 0 = rejected

A5 (14 levels) and A6 (8 levels) make this a useful test of the Multinomial margin at higher cardinality than UCI Heart Disease or Iris.

function onehot(val, levels)
    idx = findfirst(==(val), levels)
    isnothing(idx) && error("Value $val not in $levels")
    v = zeros(Int, length(levels)); v[idx] = 1; v
end

dataset = Vector{Any}(undef, 14)
dataset[1]  = Float64.(df.A2)
dataset[2]  = Float64.(df.A3)
dataset[3]  = Float64.(df.A7)
dataset[4]  = Float64.(df.A10)
dataset[5]  = Float64.(df.A13)
dataset[6]  = log1p.(Float64.(df.A14))   # log1p for extreme right skew
dataset[7]  = [onehot(x, [0, 1])              for x in df.A1]
dataset[8]  = [onehot(x, [1, 2, 3])           for x in df.A4]
dataset[9]  = [onehot(x, collect(1:14))       for x in df.A5]
dataset[10] = [onehot(x, [1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9])  for x in df.A6]
dataset[11] = [onehot(x, [0, 1])              for x in df.A8]
dataset[12] = [onehot(x, [0, 1])              for x in df.A9]
dataset[13] = [onehot(x, [0, 1])              for x in df.A11]
dataset[14] = [onehot(x, [1, 2, 3])           for x in df.A12]

# Standardize continuous features
for j in 1:6
    m = mean(dataset[j]); s = std(dataset[j])
    dataset[j] = (dataset[j] .- m) ./ s
end

labels_true = Vector{Int}(df.class)
println("Class distribution: $(count(==(1), labels_true)) approved, $(count(==(0), labels_true)) rejected")
Class distribution: 307 approved, 383 rejected

5 Fitting the Model

We fit both model settings with \(K_{\text{fit}}=10\), \(\alpha_0=0.01\).

5.1 SFRM — Shared Feature Relevance Model

Random.seed!(42)
res_sfrm = mixClust(dataset, 10;
                    model_setting = SFRM(),
                    alpha_0  = 0.01,
                    max_iter = 3000,
                    tol      = 1e-5,
                    prune    = true)

K_sfrm = size(res_sfrm.w, 2)
@printf("SFRM → K̂ = %d clusters (converged in %d / 3000 iterations)\n",
        K_sfrm, length(res_sfrm.elbo_history))
println("Cluster sizes: ", [count(==(k), res_sfrm.labels) for k in 1:K_sfrm])
SFRM → K̂ = 6 clusters (converged in 856 / 3000 iterations)
Cluster sizes: [21, 70, 71, 100, 374, 54]

5.2 LFRM — Local Feature Relevance Model

Random.seed!(42)
res_lfrm = mixClust(dataset, 10;
                    model_setting = LFRM(),
                    alpha_0  = 0.01,
                    max_iter = 3000,
                    tol      = 1e-5,
                    prune    = true)

K_lfrm = size(res_lfrm.w, 2)
@printf("LFRM → K̂ = %d clusters (converged in %d / 3000 iterations)\n",
        K_lfrm, length(res_lfrm.elbo_history))
println("Cluster sizes: ", [count(==(k), res_lfrm.labels) for k in 1:K_lfrm])

7 External Validation: A Cautionary Result

Unlike Iris, this dataset has a real binary outcome — the credit approval decision — so we can compute ARI against it. The result is worth reporting honestly.

function compute_ari(labels_true, labels_pred)
    n = length(labels_true)
    classes  = unique(labels_true)
    clusters = unique(labels_pred)
    C, K = length(classes), length(clusters)
    cont = zeros(Int, C, K)
    for i in 1:n
        ci = findfirst(==(labels_true[i]),  classes)
        ki = findfirst(==(labels_pred[i]), clusters)
        cont[ci, ki] += 1
    end
    s_ij = sum(x -> x*(x-1)/2, cont)
    s_i  = sum(x -> x*(x-1)/2, sum(cont, dims=2))
    s_j  = sum(x -> x*(x-1)/2, sum(cont, dims=1))
    exp  = (s_i * s_j) / (n*(n-1)/2)
    mx   = 0.5*(s_i + s_j)
    mx == exp && return 1.0
    return (s_ij - exp) / (mx - exp)
end

ari_sfrm = compute_ari(labels_true, res_sfrm.labels)
ari_lfrm = compute_ari(labels_true, res_lfrm.labels)

conf_sfrm = mean(maximum(res_sfrm.w[i, :]) for i in 1:nrow(df))
conf_lfrm = mean(maximum(res_lfrm.w[i, :]) for i in 1:nrow(df))

println("Summary")
println("─────────────────────────────────────────────")
@printf("  %-6s  K̂ = %d   ARI = %.3f   confidence = %.3f\n",
        "SFRM", K_sfrm, ari_sfrm, conf_sfrm)
@printf("  %-6s  K̂ = %d   ARI = %.3f   confidence = %.3f\n",
        "LFRM", K_lfrm, ari_lfrm, conf_lfrm)
Summary
─────────────────────────────────────────────
  SFRM    K̂ = 6   ARI = 0.217   confidence = 0.980
  LFRM    K̂ = 5   ARI = 0.222   confidence = 0.991

Both SFRM and LFRM score below plain K-means (K=2 fixed, ARI ≈ 0.314) — the opposite of the UCI Heart Disease result. The reason: K-means forced to \(K=2\) is by construction aligned with a binary label. Our model finds finer subpopulation structure (\(\widehat{K}=5\)–\(6\)) than the approve/reject boundary distinguishes, which mechanically incurs ARI penalties even when the finer clusters are internally coherent — as the assignment-confidence numbers above confirm.

Note

ARI against a binary label is not a fair test of automatic order selection. A finer, more confident partition that subdivides each side of the true binary decision will always be penalized by ARI against that label, even if it is a better description of the actual feature-space structure. Whether to trust the automatically selected \(\widehat{K}\) or to also check against a label-matched \(K\) depends on whether the label itself reflects the population’s true subgroup structure.

8 Does the Cluster Structure Help Downstream Prediction?

We tested two ways to exploit the discovered cluster structure for predicting loan approval, using 10-fold stratified cross-validation (Python scripts experiments/scripts/australian_predictive_cv.py and australian_moe_cv.py):

  1. Feature augmentation — soft cluster-membership weights added as extra predictors.
  2. Mixture of experts — a separate classifier per cluster, weighted by membership.
Feature set Classifier Accuracy AUC
Baseline (raw features) LogisticRegression 0.859 ± 0.049 0.928 ± 0.040
Baseline (raw features) RandomForest 0.870 ± 0.040 0.934 ± 0.040
+ SFRM cluster membership LogisticRegression 0.861 ± 0.045 0.930 ± 0.037
+ SFRM cluster membership RandomForest 0.870 ± 0.055 0.930 ± 0.042
+ LFRM cluster membership LogisticRegression 0.858 ± 0.046 0.928 ± 0.039
+ LFRM cluster membership RandomForest 0.862 ± 0.048 0.931 ± 0.042
Mixture of experts, SFRM per-cluster LogisticRegression 0.852 ± 0.053 0.910 ± 0.041
Mixture of experts, LFRM per-cluster LogisticRegression 0.852 ± 0.061 0.907 ± 0.047

Neither approach helps. Feature augmentation is a wash; the mixture of experts is slightly worse (splitting \(n=690\) into 5–6 per-cluster regressions leaves too few observations per expert). This is a useful negative result: discovering finer cluster structure does not automatically translate into better downstream prediction at this sample size.

9 Takeaways

  • MixClustVIjl handles high-cardinality categorical features (up to 14 levels) and a fully anonymized feature set without numerical difficulty.
  • LFRM surfaces features whose relevance is locally concentrated rather than uniform — consistent with the pattern found on UCI Heart Disease in the main manuscript.
  • ARI against an external label is not always going to favor automatic order selection over a fixed-\(K\) baseline — and that is not necessarily a failure of the method.
  • Discovering finer cluster structure does not automatically translate into better downstream prediction — a useful negative result for anyone tempted to assume “more structure found” implies “more useful for prediction.”
